title: Notification Service
summary: Send e-mail, SMS and push messages reliably to millions of users.
problem: Design a service other teams call to notify users by e-mail, SMS and push. It must respect user preferences and not lose or duplicate messages.
functional: Accept a notification request from internal services
Deliver through e-mail, SMS and push providers
Respect user preferences, quiet hours and unsubscribes
nonFunctional: At-least-once delivery, with deduplication so users do not get a message twice
Absorb spikes (a marketing blast of 10 million) without delaying urgent messages such as one-time passwords
Provider outages must not lose messages
constraints: Third-party providers rate limit and fail
deliverables: Requirements and the assumptions you made
A capacity estimate (requests per second, storage, bandwidth)
A high-level architecture diagram (Mermaid or an uploaded image)
The API (endpoints and payloads) and the data model
How it scales, how it fails, and what you would monitor
The main trade-offs and what you chose not to build
hints: Separate urgent from bulk traffic with different queues.
What do you store so a retry does not send twice?
reference:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Calling services] --> API[Notification API]
  API --> V[Validate + check preferences]
  V --> Q1[[Urgent queue]]
  V --> Q2[[Bulk queue]]
  Q1 --> W1[Channel workers]
  Q2 --> W2[Channel workers, rate limited]
  W1 --> P[Providers: e-mail, SMS, push]
  W2 --> P
  W1 --> DB[(Status + dedupe store)]
  W2 --> DB
  P -. webhooks .-> API
```

- Each request carries an **idempotency key**; the dedupe store ensures a retried send is not delivered twice.
- **Two priority lanes** keep a bulk campaign from delaying a login code; bulk workers are rate limited to each provider's quota.
- Workers retry with exponential backoff and jitter, then dead-letter; a second provider is the fallback.
- Preferences and unsubscribes are checked before queuing and again at send time.
- Delivery receipts come back by webhook and update the status store; scheduling uses a delayed queue.
- Be honest about the guarantee: sending to a third party is at-least-once. If a worker crashes after the provider accepted a message but before the status is recorded, the retry can send it twice, and a fallback provider can duplicate a message the first one actually delivered. Pass the idempotency key to providers that support one, and treat the dedupe store as strong protection, not a proof of exactly-once.
- Capacity (assumptions): a 10 million blast spread over an hour is about 2,800 sends/s, and a provider quota, not your own servers, is usually what sets the pace. The store keeps one row per notification per channel (50 million users x 3 messages a day = 150 million rows a day, about 30 GB a day at roughly 200 bytes a row), with old rows archived.
- Alternatives: one queue per channel and priority instead of shared worker pools; a managed provider (or provider-side batching APIs) for bulk e-mail instead of running your own sender.
